seoTitle: Plant Spacing Calculator - Garden Layout Tool
metaDescription: Free online Plant Spacing Calculator. Calculate exactly how many plants, shrubs, or trees you can fit in your garden bed based on grid or triangular spacing.
secondaryKeywords: how many plants do I need
intro: Planning a new hedge or a vegetable garden? Our free Plant Spacing Calculator ensures you don't over-purchase at the nursery by determining exactly how many plants will fit in your space.
whatIs: The Plant Spacing Calculator is an agricultural and landscaping layout tool. It calculates the maximum capacity of a designated planting area based on the required physical distance between each plant's root system.
howToUse: Enter the length and width of your garden bed.
Enter the required spacing distance between plants (e.g., 12 inches).
Select your layout pattern (Square/Grid or Triangular/Hexagonal).
The tool instantly outputs the maximum number of plants you can fit.
howItWorks: For a Square layout, the tool divides the area's length by the spacing distance, then the width by the spacing, and multiplies the two numbers. For a Triangular layout (which staggers the rows like a honeycomb), the tool applies a multiplier (usually 1.15) to calculate the denser packing capacity.
workedExample: A 10ft by 10ft garden bed (120x120 inches). You want to plant tomatoes that require 24 inches of space. 120 / 24 = 5 plants per row. 5 rows × 5 columns = 25 total plants in a square grid.
resultInterpretation: The result is your exact nursery shopping list. Sticking to this number prevents overcrowding, which can lead to stunted growth, fungal diseases due to poor airflow, and root competition.
useCases: Vegetable Gardening: Figuring out how many pepper or tomato plants can safely fit in a new raised wooden planter box.
Landscaping: Calculating how many Boxwood shrubs are required to form a dense, continuous privacy hedge along a 50-foot property line.
Farming: Agricultural planning to determine seed purchasing requirements for a one-acre cash crop.
tipsAndLimitations: Triangular (staggered) spacing is more efficient and allows you to fit up to 15% more plants in the exact same area without violating the root spacing requirements.
Always leave a 'border gap' of at least half the spacing distance between the edge of your bed and the first row of plants so they don't spill out.

faq.question: What is triangular spacing?
faq.answer: Instead of planting in a perfect square grid like a chessboard, triangular spacing shifts every other row so the plants sit in the empty gaps of the previous row, forming a honeycomb pattern.

faq.question: How do I know what the spacing should be?
faq.answer: Every seed packet or nursery plant tag will list a 'Spacing' requirement (e.g., 18 inches). This is the distance required for the mature plant to be healthy.

disclaimer: The calculator provides strict geometric capacities. Always refer to specific plant tags for unique growth habits and sunlight requirements.
